figs.title: Wild Types
figs.caption: Natural selection (I), predation (II), and non-selective planting (III). Abscission shifts to shattering once humans harvest.

figs.title: Genes Under Selection
figs.caption: Selective harvesting drives a trait down; selective planting drives it up. Rows = genes, columns = harvest/plant × max/min.

figs.title: Domesticated Variants
figs.caption: The domesticated (non-shattering) subpopulation from the five selective-planting experiments that produced one; red box = directly-selected gene.

figs.title: Wild Variants
figs.caption: Three selective-planting experiments that stayed wild; selecting the shattering (max abscission) trait is indistinguishable from wild, so no isolation begins.

figs.title: Sickle Theory
figs.caption: Harvesting non-shattering seeds (a sickle) does not domesticate: vs Wild Type II (no planting) and Wild Type III (+ random planting), the sickle barely shifts the population from wild.

figs.title: Unintended Selective Planting
figs.caption: Replanting the first-harvested seeds domesticates via geographic selection: total / wild / domesticated.

figs.title: Lineage-Age Planting
figs.caption: Planting the freshest lineage (no trait selection) reproductively isolates and domesticates the crop: total / wild / domesticated — the isolation mechanism in isolation.

figs.title: Planting effort × population
figs.caption: Domestication (left) beside lineage divergence (right): human population × swept parameter. Divergence = TV distance between the planted and harvested lineage-age distributions.

figs.title: The collapse — domestication vs lineage divergence
figs.caption: Each point is one setting: corrected domestication vs lineage divergence (TV between planted and harvested lineage-age distributions), colored by sweep. Colored lines are per-sweep binned means (legend gives each sweep’s Pearson r); the black line is the pooled binned mean. All sweeps trend together — energy is the weakest.
